items.question: How did your research interests evolve from computer vision benchmarks toward representation learning?
items.object: The evolution of research interests from computer vision benchmarks to representation learning
items.answer: I was actually rather lost when I went to CUHK, because although AI was popular then, I didn’t know what I really liked doing. So I tried many directions. CUHK was especially strong at detection, segmentation, and classification, and they had won many championships. But personally, I wasn’t very interested in leaderboard-chasing—just looking at one number, frankly. Then generative adversarial networks became popular. I found it interesting because it could genuinely generate an image for people to see. You could even do simple editing. So I chose to continue in generative models. I started working on them early, from 2017. As influential work emerged, especially the StyleGAN series, image editing became popular—adjusting an image as you wanted, such as making yourself prettier. But I gradually felt that was too far downstream, so I wondered whether we could move earlier than editing. That is what people would now call pretraining. There was not really that concept then. Put simply, I wanted to train the generative model. But as we trained it, it felt increasingly outside our control. There was no talk yet of scaling parameter counts, and we didn’t know how to make the model better. So I moved one step earlier, from generation to representations. Step by step, I went from not being interested in numbers, to being interested in generated content, then from editing to underlying training, and then further forward to representation learning. That was basically the path.

items.question: How do you assess the value of continuing to scale up generative adversarial networks (GANs)?
items.object: The value and limits of scaling up generative adversarial networks (GANs)
items.answer: That’s an interesting story. Even early this year, we made one last attempt. Even after diffusion became popular, and later people began using autoregression for generation, our team still persisted with GAN scale-up for a while. It did achieve some results. A GAN model we made recently will be released. Compared with diffusion, it is indeed weaker in some respects, but it is still much improved over technology from previous years. So it has value, but its biggest problem is poor computational efficiency. Diffusion can iterate many times to generate an image. For especially complex content—particularly video generation, where there is simply so much content—GANs may truly not be the best choice. So we may consolidate the techniques we accumulated with GANs, release them publicly, and consider that the end of the chapter. I wouldn’t call it perfect, but it is a conclusion. We probably will not make many more attempts in the GAN setup. But GANs’ core technique is adversarial learning: training two models that iteratively interact and compete. We accumulated some experience there. Apart from GANs themselves, I think that technique will still be useful later.

items.question: Why did you feel that computer vision’s potential in the digital world was limited enough to consider moving into robotics?
items.object: Computer vision’s industrial potential and the move into robotics
items.answer: I was in computer vision. Frankly, over the past decade or so—I think the first wave was facial recognition. That was certainly a major application. The second may have been autonomous driving, popularized by Tesla and its pure-vision approach. Beyond that, we had not really seen a visual application used at massive scale with strong industrial value. That is why, in 2024, I began wanting to move from vision into robotics: vision did not seem to have enough room to play a central role in the digital world.

items.question: How did you think about your decision to pursue embodied intelligence at Ant Lingbo?

People often associate Ant with finance, but it also does many services in healthcare, mobility, and so on—many lifestyle services in the digital world. At the Group level, extending those services further naturally meant moving into the physical world. At the end of 2024, Ant formally announced the establishment of a subsidiary. items.object: Establishing a subsidiary dedicated to embodied intelligence
items.answer: I think it reflected a major commitment by the Group. items.question: Why do you see your work at Ant Lingbo as an opportunity to do something substantial?
items.object: Ant Lingbo’s opportunity to combine innovation with industrial value in robotics
items.answer: At ByteDance I was doing business work. At Ant’s Institute of Technology, I happened to experience the period before large models and then their explosion, which was a shock. I became confused: what is good research? Does publishing a paper or getting many citations mean you are successful? What value are we bringing, whether to academia on a smaller scale or industry on a larger one? I was not very clear internally. At Ant Lingbo, my feeling is much stronger: it combines the two. We want to do things differently, but those things also directly face real needs. Why is now a good opportunity? We are still doing business, but robot technology has not converged. As technologists, we can contribute to the industry at this stage—even exploring an incorrect path is a contribution. There is much to do while the technology has not converged. So if you want to do something substantial now, but do not want to be on a completely uninnovative, purely certain path—just driving the stakes deeper—I think today is a good opportunity instead. People have room to contribute here while doing things of value to industry.

items.question: Why do you see the robot-brain layer as the right focus for Lingbo?
items.object: Lingbo’s strategy of developing the robot-brain layer
items.answer: Let me first explain our original intention. When we were founded, we followed Ant Group’s vision of inclusiveness and the expansion of its lifestyle services. Ultimately, we hope that one day every household will have a robot. But nobody knows what that robot will look like, or whether it will necessarily be from one brand. Phones today come in all varieties. We hope every household will eventually have a robot running Lingbo’s model—using Lingbo’s brain. We will also make things such as end effectors, because models have not fully converged and we do not know what embodied hardware will become. Just as phones are not all one fixed brand—not everyone uses Apple or Huawei—we have no definite answer here. But our clear idea is that these embodiments should run on a Lingbo brain. So we are firmly following this path, first blazing it and making it solid. That is our overall thinking.

items.question: How do you think research and real-world deployment should shape each other at Lingbo?
items.object: The relationship between research and deployment at Lingbo
items.answer: As I said, because industry technology has not converged, there must be a research component. In other words, we must continually explore where the upper limit of intelligence lies, and that exploration itself is research. But because we chose from the beginning to operate as a company, we do not want the research to become too unconstrained. We want it to be strongly connected to industry. So we essentially pursue both: explore intelligence’s upper limit, and pursue deployment. We must test in real application scenarios, find what does not work, and use those failures in reverse to drive which directions the next model iteration should take. Models are still early; there may be eight or ten, or even more, directions to iterate on, but resources are limited. You cannot pursue everything. Which feature gets developed first is therefore determined by industry or deployment.

items.question: Why did you decide that robots needed to learn temporal information from video?
items.object: Lingbo’s 2025 decision to train robots on temporal information in video
items.answer: Around March 2025, we realized that robots were not merely about multimodal understanding. They have to move and interact with the environment. We realized that dynamic modeling, or temporal modeling, would be crucial for robotics going forward. There was not yet a technical route called WAM—vision-action model—at that time, but we firmly believed robots had to learn from video: not extracting frames and treating them as images, but truly learning temporal information. We made that bold decision early in 2025. After roughly nine months, early this year, 2026, we were among the first—perhaps the first in the industry, I think—to release and open-source what people now call a visual-action model. We call it a visual-action model. VA. I think that was a major decision in 2025.

items.question: Why did you decide to rebuild your robotics models entirely around physical-world needs?
items.object: Building robotics models entirely around physical-world needs
items.answer: We saw an important problem: the original purpose of developing digital-world models is not necessarily well matched to physical-world needs. Yet we could not push their developers to change, because the digital world has its own logic and application scenarios. For example, video generation wants especially high image quality—that is a digital-world need. For robot actions in the physical world, it is not that important. We could not push them to change their models because they had their own iteration pace. So this year—or this half-year—we made a major decision: since we could not push them to change, we would redo everything based entirely on physical-world needs.

items.question: What led you to commit Lingbo to learning from real sensors and video in a way native to the physical world?
items.object: Lingbo’s commitment to sensor-based, video-based learning native to the physical world
items.answer: We also made another major decision in 2025. The first major decision was that we had to model video. Another was that we were firmly committed to starting from real sensors to solve physical-world problems. This was connected to my naïveté when I first came to Lingbo at the end of 2024: I thought moving things to robots would be easy. We initially tried using many digital-world algorithms and computer-vision models directly on robots, and found deployment completely different from what we had imagined. I had done a lot of research, and academia has an implicit convention—perhaps not a bad one—that datasets are relatively clean. You rarely see very noisy data in datasets. But in real applications, robots operate in the real world, and sensor noise simply cannot be ignored. That is inherently at odds with getting clean data. So in 2025, we insisted on starting at the sensor level. That includes vision and perhaps touch. Those are Lingbo’s two major technical propositions: start from sensors—what people now more readily understand as spatial intelligence—and insist on learning from video. And learn from scratch in a way native to the physical world. Those are the two major propositions.

items.question: Why do you think a general-purpose robot brain should work across different embodiments from the outset?
items.object: A general-purpose robot brain that works across different embodiments
items.answer: Our original intention was to make a general-purpose brain. By “general-purpose,” we judged that the industry needs robots that may eventually enter homes, though there may first be B2B stages. We think it is hard for one robot to truly fit every task. Even once robots enter homes, each home may have different needs. From a task perspective, it is unlikely in the short term that one general-purpose embodiment will solve everything. Since our main business is brains, we start with brains. We have always advocated that our brain should be cross-embodiment from the outset—general-purpose. That is why we included data from different embodiments in training. We hope the brain experiences these embodiments during pretraining and understands their characteristics, so it can quickly adapt to one in a real deployment scenario. That technical route is consistent with our broader corporate strategy of making a general-purpose brain.

items.question: Why did you choose those four robotics models for open source in January 2026?

items.answer: In 2025, our two decisions were to learn from video and to do spatial intelligence—starting from sensors. items.question: How did trying to deploy VRA change your understanding of what a robot brain needs to control?
items.object: The control requirements of a robot brain in real-world VRA deployment
items.answer: Our first-generation brain supported nine configurations and could do relatively simple grasping tasks. That was also the type of action the industry was doing most at the time, and it handled some grasping relatively well. As we engaged with the industry and deployment, that led to a fundamental change in this generation of models. When we actually tried to deploy VRA, we found a point people had not paid much attention to. Previous demos were mostly laboratory environments, with operations performed on tabletops. But in real scenarios, robots perform many actions at non-fixed heights. For instance, retrieving something from a shelf requires raising an arm. When it raises its arm, the gap between laboratory and real deployment becomes clear: should the head look toward where the hand is raised? The viewpoint differs, and even if the head is raised, it may still not see. Can the model control head-raising? If the head camera fails, can it do the task using only wrist cameras or other sensors? In pretraining the earliest, first version of the model, we supported only arm degrees of freedom and grippers—no head or anything else. The nine configurations were for simple tabletop manipulation tasks.

items.question: How do you assess the value of simulation data for robotics models?
items.object: Simulation data for training and evaluating robotics models
items.answer: We use simulation more for evaluation; we generally do not use simulated data to train models. Simulation can generate a huge volume of data, but beyond quantity, distribution is crucial. Distribution includes, for example, embodiment configuration as one distribution and task dimensions as another. Simulation can undoubtedly generate huge amounts instantly in areas it is good at. But from another perspective, its distribution may be more severely homogeneous. It may do similar tasks. For things such as soft-body simulation, or tearing open a plastic bag, I think physics engines still need time for further iteration. After upgrades, simulation data may be more useful. But for tasks simulation currently handles well—grasping and moving things, for example—the cost of real-robot data has also been gradually declining across the industry.

items.question: What do you see as the core know-how in preparing training data for cross-embodiment robot models?
items.object: Training-data preparation for cross-embodiment robot models
items.answer: You cannot have 90 percent of the data never using the head and only 10 percent using it. A better example: if head degrees of freedom occur far more often than waist degrees of freedom, the model may tend to learn the head and barely move the waist. That is the intuitive way I understand it. Another piece of know-how is how to clean the data after you obtain it—the entire pipeline. We spent a long time dealing with that, because there is an inherent difficulty: we make cross-embodiment models. Each embodiment has different characteristics, so many data-processing methods need to be closely related to the embodiment. You cannot really process every embodiment with one universal data pipeline. Camera placement may differ, as may the number of joint degrees of freedom and their connections—the configuration. Those hardware-configuration differences make data processing very difficult. So the two core pieces of know-how are task assignment and cleaning data once it has been collected.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between a robotic manipulation task’s complexity and its generality?
items.object: Generality of robotic manipulation tasks
items.answer: Generally, I’d say the simpler the manipulation, the better its generality. That may depend on operator ability. The more complex a task is, the fewer data-collection operators can complete it fully and smoothly. If an operator’s movement during collection is not smooth, you generally cannot edit it into being smooth afterward; it is one data trajectory, and that cost is enormous. If you cannot smooth it out, the trained model may believe that is the correct way to operate. Then the robot may also be very jerky when controlling it.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between Lingbo Vision and Lingbo Depth?
items.object: The relationship between Lingbo Vision and Lingbo Depth
items.answer:
I think this is something we did well this time. Let me first explain the relationship, then why. On day one, we released two models: Vision, namely Lingbo Vision, and an upgrade of Lingbo Depth. In version 1.0, our Depth was based on DINO; we used DINOv2 as the pretrained model. DINOv2 is also, in a sense, a digital-world model, particularly good at semantic understanding. But in the digital world, semantic understanding is often enough: knowing this is a pot of flowers or a dog. We found that semantic-level pretraining does not naturally align with truly understanding space or distance. So we redid pretraining ourselves. Unlike DINO, this time the pretraining modeling starts entirely from geometry. You can understand geometry roughly as points, lines, and planes—or edges. We start from edges to help the model understand geometry better. Geometry is closely related to distance.

So with this Vision model, we updated the underlying base model and found a major improvement over using DINOv2 for depth. After half a year of accumulation, our data volume also multiplied several times. So we iterated Depth again using our own new base model and more data.

There are several interesting examples. The first one shocked me: a reflective kitchen faucet with the water turned on. We can clearly see the water stream. This is critical if a robot truly wants to execute a task: to fill water, it must first be able to see the water. It has to see where the water is—not merely whether the water is on, but where the stream is. Previously, it likely knew the water was running, but its distance estimate was definitely inaccurate. Depth trained from our Vision can do this.

The second is even more vivid, and I like using it to explain why semantic understanding in the digital world differs from distance in the physical world. Imagine a balcony with a glass door and a cat outside. Our new Depth model cannot see the cat at all, because a sheet of glass blocks it. If a person walks forward, they will hit the glass first. Only then is there the cat. So when we try to pull the glass door open, the cat in the Depth output gradually emerges from behind the door. Because the glass has been pulled aside, it can see the cat. But from a semantic-understanding standpoint, the cat was there all along. The digital world only needs to know there is a cat. In the physical world, you also need to know there is a door in front of you. I think this is an excellent example: you can see it, but cannot touch it. Being able to see it is semantic understanding; being unable to touch it is spatial perception.

Their relationship is that Vision is Depth’s pretraining. Previously, Depth used DINO for pretraining. Now we do not use DINO. We built a new pretraining pipeline ourselves. You can understand it as a strong understanding of vision itself—that is what pretraining does. Depth is its downstream task: how to transform visual perception into spatial perception. In effect, it transforms images into 3D. That is roughly the relationship.

items.question: How do you see the fit between models developed for the digital world and the needs of robots in the physical world?
items.object: The mismatch between digital-world model development and physical-world needs
items.answer: With version 1.0, we found that the development motivations of many digital-world models did not match physical-world needs. There are several obvious mismatches. First, in the digital world, especially video generation or what people now like to call world models, visual compression is done before video generation because the final image quality must be very high. To do that, it must first compress. But commonly available open-source compression is just compression: it has no help or connection to downstream learning. Roughly speaking, it might turn something of size 100 into 30 so it is easier to learn. This time, to help robots better understand semantics and actions during subsequent learning, we added semantic and action alignment while training that visual-compression model. In other words, during encoding, this compressor—or encoder—can perceive some semantic and action information. With such an encoder, when it later learns generation based on encoded representations, it can understand semantics and action better. That is one point. The second difference between the digital and physical worlds is that the digital world does not care much about efficiency. For example, with text-to-video, I give it text and it returns a video. If it takes 30 seconds to generate a 30-second video, the user can wait 30 seconds—or 10 or 20 seconds.

items.question: How do you think the demands of real-time robotics change the design priorities for generation models compared with digital-world video generation?
items.object: Physical-world generation models for real-time robotics
items.answer: I see two requirements, because it must be real-time—absolutely real-time. First: can your model be made faster? People may use Wan more now. Wan is a dense model; it does not use an MoE form. For example, if it is a 14B model, all 14B are activated at inference. Even if downstream acceleration work is excellent, if the model’s activation itself is not accelerated architecturally, the proportion you can speed up is fixed; you cannot make it extremely fast. That is one point. Another is that because it is real-time, it must use so-called unidirectional modeling. The past cannot see the future; the future can see the past. But the past cannot see the future. Time flows in one direction. For digital-world generation models, it can be bidirectional. You give it text and wait; during that wait, it effectively knows both the beginning and ending of the video and can simply give you a complete video. It does not have to move forward only as it goes. These are relatively new physical-world requirements. But this does not only make things harder; the physical world also permits trade-offs. The core thing that can be sacrificed is image quality. The digital world demands high definition and high frame rates so content looks good and is enjoyable; that is especially true for content generation.

items.question: What do you see as the real technical challenge in training Lingbo-Video’s native MoE architecture?
items.object: Training the native MoE architecture of Lingbo-Video
items.answer: Lingbo-Video, which we also open-sourced, is a natively MoE-architecture model. People may think MoE simply means turning a dense model into one where not everything activates every time—say, activating one out of three parameters. But properly training MoE is difficult. During training, you must ensure the activation proportion for each generation is balanced. If there are 30 parameters and the same 10 are activated every time, the other 20 are almost never activated. That is unacceptable. In that case it is no different from a 10B dense model, or a dense model with ten parameters. If we want sparsity, we need it to be uniformly sparse. How to train an MoE so that each parameter is activated uniformly—roughly with the same probability—and train it well is a technical problem. It is not an easy problem; you cannot simply decide to activate less and do so. So for Video, since we trained from scratch ourselves, I think we have now worked through and figured out this MoE problem.

items.question: Why did you decide to train unidirectional attention from scratch rather than convert a bidirectional pretrained model?
items.object: Training unidirectional attention from scratch rather than converting a bidirectional pretrained model
items.answer: Time cannot run backward. By that, I mean we require the entire attention mechanism to be unidirectional. Attention, or models commonly used in the digital world, are basically bidirectional, because they require image quality. With bidirectionality, the more connections there are in the middle, the more computation you have; and more computation definitely gives better results. That is certain. But we wanted to make it unidirectional. We had hoped to do that since version 1.0, and we probably spent another three or four months on it, until we could train unidirectionally from scratch. There is another option: first have a bidirectional model, then turn it into a unidirectional one. We found a major problem in that process: some knowledge learned by pretrained models, such as their understanding of text, is embedded in their bidirectional attention. Some knowledge is implicit there. When we forcibly make it unidirectional, the unidirectional setup works, but some of that knowledge is forgotten. It is as though pretraining has been invalidated. An intuitive sign is that before, we could give it one hundred sentences and it could translate every one into a reasonably good video. Now, if we give it one hundred sentences, perhaps only 20 or 30 percent translate into good videos. For the other seventy sentences, it no longer understands what we are saying, because that knowledge has been damaged. So in turning bidirectional into unidirectional, we made a fairly major decision: decisively abandoning that route and designing it to be unidirectional from the very beginning. The Video work solved the MoE issue—training MoE from scratch, giving us the ability to train MoE. The Word work proved that we could also solve unidirectional-attention training. We ultimately applied all these techniques to the embodied model with huge numbers of parameters. That gave rise to the model we released on the final day: VA 2.0.

items.question: What do you mean by an “embodied-native” foundation model for robots?

items.answer: Video was our proof that we could make MoE work—we first blazed that trail. Then Word blazed the trail for causal pretraining. For example, suppose you wake up in the morning and the robot opens the curtains for you; it knows to do that. items.question: What do you see as the major improvements from designing your second-generation robot’s model specifically for embodiment?
items.object: The second-generation robot’s embodiment-specific model
items.answer: Rather than continuing to iterate on models from the digital world, we designed a model specifically for embodiment. That has led to several major and interesting improvements. First, it is now much better at handling randomness and random situations. We have a demo where it plays a kind of ball game with a person. That demo is different from the usual ones because there is strong randomness: you never know where the thing the person hits toward you will be. I am not saying we arrange all the positions and then it is done. It has to see the ball come toward it before it can return it. And a key point is that throughout the process, we rely only on the robot’s own cameras. We did not place a ring of cameras around the court to track the object’s position. Another thing is that the exchanges are very fast. Because it is playing with a person, it has very high real-time requirements. It is not something where the robot can move slowly, or move a little, lag, move a little, lag. In that case it cannot return the ball.

items.question: How do you assess the improvement in your 2.0 robot model’s ability to learn tasks compared with 1.0?

items.question: How do you see embodied intelligence’s relationship to large language models as a field develops its own models?
items.object: Embodied intelligence’s relationship to large language models
items.answer: I cannot say completely that I belong to either camp—whether embodiment is a branch growing from LLMs or an independent direction. If I had to choose, I would probably choose the latter. The problems embodied intelligence needs to solve do not conflict with those of language models. Language models are more about enabling people and robots to understand what an instruction means. Embodied intelligence needs more to solve how to do something well; doing it well does not itself require understanding language again. But the preceding step—translating language into the subsequent sequence of actions—may rely on language models. I believe embodiment will continue to use large language models as a good entry point. Then it will grow its own model. The two may only interact at an interface layer. Of course, better still would be to embed the language system within embodiment. But in the short term, the problem embodied intelligence should focus on is not that; it first needs to solve how to do a task properly. Personally, I think doing a task properly does not depend on language that heavily.

items.question: How do you assess the pace of robotics hardware development since you started your company at the end of 2024?

items.answer: I think it has progressed much faster than I expected. That is one point. Since last year, everyone had grippers; this year, dexterous-hand companies have begun springing up everywhere. There are already many dexterous-hand companies, and their development is such that I do not think it will take too long before they gradually become standard equipment. Gradually, of course—it still needs time, because hardware has its own development cycle. But people are already dissatisfied with grippers. Also, there are increasingly many tactile sensors. Dexterous hands and touch are for enabling robots to do more complex and finer-grained tasks. In terms of hardware itself, or hardware development in this industry, that pace has been quite astonishing to me.

items.question: How do you understand the shift toward building robot brains instead of robot bodies?
items.object: Robot body design and companies’ shift toward robot brains
items.answer: I think a key point is that, at present, a robot body is hard to make universal. If it is not universal, you have to choose the right scenario for it to make sense to build the body. The body is designed specifically for that scenario. Such specialization lets you reinforce some things and simplify others, because deployment ultimately comes down to cost. We cannot take an all-around “hexagonal warrior” and use it for one specific task. Many things would be overconfigured, and costs would rise. One reason people may not talk about the body is, first, that bodies have their own barriers: can you actually mass-produce them? Second, if you choose the scenario incorrectly, the body design will definitely have problems. But scenarios are difficult right now. No one really dares to say which scenario will definitely work extremely well; everyone is experimenting. It may indeed be difficult to determine which scenario will be the first to take off.

items.question: How do you think AI model requirements should shape the next generation of robotic sensors?
items.object: Model-driven upgrades to robotic sensors, especially tactile sensors
items.answer: I think the hardware itself may be okay, but sensors, especially tactile sensors, probably still need further upgrades. For example, touch sensors—or sensors generally—used to have metrics: precision must reach a given level, frequency must reach a given level, and so on. If you only make the sensor, you naturally want all those metrics to be good. But sometimes you cannot make everything excellent, so there must be trade-offs. What to give up and what to retain is a question. Previously, people might decide from use cases—for instance, force needs to be accurate, so a tactile sensor should prioritize force accuracy. That is perhaps an instinctive assumption. But in the AI era, what the model most needs may not be accurate force; it may need fast response. I may have higher requirements for real-time performance. All of that is possible. So if sensors are upgraded, it may need to begin with model requirements: which metrics should we strengthen and which should we weaken? We have not reached the point where models can define them. Sensor development still follows the traditional understanding of how to optimize as much as possible. I think this may be a future trend.

items.question: Why do you see moving from architecture-native to data-native design as the biggest next step for your robot foundation model?
items.object: Moving from architecture-native to data-native robot foundation models
items.answer: I think this: in this round, we made some native designs based on physical characteristics. Next, the biggest step is to move further from architecture-native toward data-native. items.question: How do you think about balancing data quality and scalability for embodied-intelligence models?

items.answer: I think we need data that are scalable and usable by models. “Usable by models” is important. Usability and scalability are themselves a balance, because models naturally want data to be as good as possible, with as high quality as possible. They want as many modalities as possible. items.question: How do you think about the gamble involved in developing native models?
items.object: Developing native models
items.answer: I think native models are a big bet. With native models, you may get to the end and find you cannot make them. Entering too early can be a problem. Insufficient resources are another issue: perhaps you can only do a 100-yuan job but insist on doing a 200-yuan job. You do not have enough resources. items.question: How do you assess the progress of your physical-world-native model against your expectations?

items.answer: Actually, it was somewhat above expectations. We talk about being native in two major areas. One is vision—seeing more clearly. I think this part has been pushed forward a step by being native. The other is thinking more clearly, which we also pushed a step further through native design: architecture-native, whether it is the passage of time, inference efficiency, and so on. Then there is doing things more deftly. I think that may be the next kind of native design: data-native. Once data can be scaled better, there will certainly be a better breakthrough in task generalization. Then the physical world would truly have its own complete system, from model to architecture—to data. A closed-loop native system.

items.question: How do you think the competitive landscape for robot intelligence models will develop?
items.object: The competitive landscape for robot intelligence models
items.answer: I think the landscape may resemble that of large language models: some big companies will do well, and two or three startups will also do well. I think we are currently closer to a startup. But our position is special: we are a startup backed by a large company. For the intelligence layer, I think that is roughly the landscape: one or two major-company players, and two or three startup players. Then each may develop its own ecosystem, including data ecosystems, body ecosystems, and scenario ecosystems. Once you have an ecosystem, your scenarios and bodies provide data within it, and your model may gradually differentiate to better fit that ecosystem. Of course, everyone may ultimately move toward a general ecosystem—entering homes. Before that, each model may have different characteristics. Some may suit delicate tasks, while others may suit long-horizon tasks. It is hard to say. But I think it will be a landscape with several leading players, each with its own characteristics.
